stories.title: CRE Liquidity Is Closing the Gap Between Capital and Deals
stories.excerpt: JLL’s recently released Global Bid and Credit Intensity Indices shows that credit markets are supporting transaction velocity, investor conviction is overcoming macroeconomic uncertainty and lenders continue competing to place capital. The gap between the indices peaked in May 2026 and has steadily narrowed since, “indicating stronger alignment between financing availability and transaction execution,” JLL said. Investor Implications Here’s what the data means for investors: Open liquidity window. Capital markets have moved beyond recovery and into expansion, JLL said. Buyers are benefiting from competitive financing terms that remain historically attractive despite recent yield movements. At the same time, sellers are seeing more investors with greater certainty of deal execution. Better borrower leverage. Increased lender competition is creating “tangible advantages in deal structuring, pricing and terms,” JLL said. Despite recent increases in Treasury and bond yields, the cost of capital and overall credit environment remain favorable. Sustainable market alignment. Liquidity and sales markets are becoming better aligned, creating a functionally healthier market. “Buyers can underwrite with greater confidence in financing execution,” JLL said, while sellers start transactions with deeper bidder pools. Lenders, meanwhile, are able to originate loans with greater visibility into refinancing strategies. What to Look for in H2 2026 JLL described current conditions as a “rare combination” of deep liquidity, competitive financing and motivated buyers and sellers. The Bid and Credit Intensity indices suggest that this environment could persist through the end of the year. Still, macroeconomic pressures remain. “Decisiveness will increasingly differentiate successful execution from missed opportunities,” JLL said. bullets: JLL indices show gap between capital availability and deal execution peaked May 2026, now narrowing steadily.
Lenders competing to place capital; borrowers gaining tangible advantages in leverage, pricing, and terms.
Capital markets moved into expansion; Treasury yields up but cost of capital remains historically attractive.
stories.summary: JLL's Global Bid and Credit Intensity Indices show the gap between available capital and transaction execution peaked in May 2026 and has steadily narrowed, signaling stronger market alignment. Lenders are competing aggressively to place capital, giving borrowers better pricing and structuring flexibility despite recent bond yield increases. Capital markets have moved beyond recovery into expansion, with buyers underwriting with greater confidence and sellers seeing deeper bidder pools.
stories.impact: Tightening capital-deal gap directly benefits multifamily developers: financing certainty and lender competition enable larger, more aggressive underwriting for acquisitions and ground-up starts across all major metros. Favorable borrowing terms and expanded leverage create a wider window to secure funding for pipeline projects before cap rates stabilize or compress further.

stories.title: Cold Storage Faces a Transition as Long-Term Demand Continues Building
stories.excerpt: The U.S. cold-storage market is navigating a near-term supply-demand imbalance, posting negative net absorption during the first six months of 2026. On the other hand, the sector’s long-term demand fundamentals remain intact. Newmark’s 1H 2026 Cold Storage Market Overview pointed to population growth, domestic food production, e-grocery and increasingly sophisticated pharmaceutical and biologics supply chains as key demand drivers. Meanwhile, occupiers are becoming more selective, putting older facilities at a disadvantage as tenants favor modern, higher-quality product. Focus on Facilities Approximately 41 million cubic feet of cold-storage space was delivered in 1H 2026, while net absorption stood at 56 million cubic feet, resulting in a 7.7% vacancy rate. But bifurcation is the trend. Facilities delivered since 2020 have generated higher demand, while older legacy properties experienced negative absorption since 2022. Those vintage assets account for 68% of vacancy, compared with 24% for post-2020 product. High construction costs that range from $130 to $350 per square foot are also a challenge. Newmark said increased costs and longer construction timelines mean new cold-storage projects are likely to be build-to-suit, owner-user or pre-leased developments. Meanwhile, lower conversion costs of $100 to $150 per square foot could spur repositioning of older dry-warehouse stock, Newmark said. Grocery Creates a Headwind Although food prices have moderated from their 2020-2022 surge, they remain more than 30% above 2019 levels. Consumers also faced pressure from reduced SNAP benefits and a gas-price spike since March 2026, further squeezing food budgets, Newmark said. Performance varies by category. Grocery unit sales fell 1.8% year over year, with fresh produce among the hardest-hit. bullets: Cold-storage market posted negative net absorption in 1H 2026; 41M SF delivered versus 56M SF absorbed.
Bifurcation: post-2020 facilities generating higher demand; legacy properties account for 68% of vacancy, newer product only 24%.
High construction costs ($130–$350/SF) forcing shift to build-to-suit, owner-user, and pre-leased models.
stories.summary: The U.S. cold-storage sector is experiencing a near-term supply-demand imbalance with negative net absorption in the first half of 2026, though long-term demand drivers—population growth, e-grocery, pharmaceutical supply chains—remain intact. The market is bifurcating sharply: facilities delivered since 2020 are absorbing well, while legacy properties (68% of vacancies) struggle. Construction costs ranging from $130 to $350 per square foot are pushing new cold-storage development toward build-to-suit and pre-leased models.
stories.impact: Not directly relevant to multifamily development, though the bifurcation trend and occupier selectivity signal that older assets lose value quickly when oversupplied. The shift toward build-to-suit in logistics underscores tighter, quality-focused occupancy markets—a reminder that aging multifamily stock in secondary/tertiary markets faces similar pressure without capital reinvestment.

stories.title: Harrison Street, Meridian Buy 431K SF NoVA Office Portfolio
stories.excerpt: Meridian Group and Harrison Street Asset Management have acquired a five-building office portfolio in Chantilly, Va., as part of a broader push to attract national security, defense and intelligence firms as tenants. The joint venture, which also includes HLM Associates, acquired the Stoneleigh and Newbrook campuses totaling 431,000 square feet in the Westfields submarket of Fairfax County. The buyers said they plan additional capital investments to expand secure-facility capabilities and to modernize infrastructure across the portfolio. The companies did not disclose pricing. Bisnow reported the sale price at approximately $67 million, citing a source familiar with the deal. The five properties are at 4800 and 4840 Westfields Boulevard and 14150, 14151 and 14155 Newbrook Drive. An affiliate of the RMR Group sold the properties, records show. The acquisition is the first for Meridian’s platform around secure, mission-critical facilities, according to Gary Block, the Bethesda-based firm’s chief investment officer. “Our goal is to become a landlord of choice for both traditional government contractors and the growing universe of nontraditional defense and technology companies in the markets we serve,” Block said in a statement. Harrison Street, which has approximately $109 billion in assets under management, said the strategy targets specialized properties benefiting from government-related demand and high barriers to entry. HLM also has expertise in the development and operation of facilities supporting classified government operations. Gregory Cornfield can be reached at gcornfield@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Harrison Street, Meridian, HLM acquired 431K SF Stoneleigh/Newbrook office portfolio in Chantilly, Va. for ~$67M.
Joint venture targeting secure-facility capabilities for national security, defense, intelligence tenant recruitment.
Westfields submarket (Fairfax County) focus reflects Northern Virginia's government-defense contracting strength and tenant demand.
stories.summary: Harrison Street Asset Management, Meridian Group, and HLM Associates acquired a five-building, 431,000-square-foot office portfolio in Chantilly, Virginia (Westfields submarket, Fairfax County) for approximately $67 million. The acquisition marks Meridian's first platform focused on secure, mission-critical facilities. The joint venture plans capital investments to expand secure-facility capabilities and modernize infrastructure to attract national security, defense, and intelligence tenants.
stories.impact: Not directly relevant to multifamily development. However, the deal signals concentrated investor interest in defense/intel office assets in Northern Virginia—a sector-specific capital flow that competes for capital in the NoVA market but does not directly affect multifamily demand, supply, or financing dynamics.

stories.title: 814K-SF Spartanburg Industrial Park Trades for $99.5M
stories.excerpt: Brennan Investment Group and Grandview Partners sold Crossroads Logistics Park, an 814,000 square foot industrial campus in Spartanburg, SC. The sales price was $99.5 million. Commercial Search reports that Invesco Real Estate acquired the asset. The campus was 100% occupied at the time of the sale. The average remaining lease term exceeds five years. Crossroads Logistics Park, 151 International Park Drive, comprises two 168,480-square-foot facilities and a 477,360-square-foot warehouse. Spanning 70 acres, the campus is close to Interstate 85, known as South Carolina’s Upstate logistics corridor, which connects Charlotte, N.C., and Atlanta and covers 10 counties. Brennan Investment Group started construction in March 2022, with J.M. Cope Construction as general contractor. JLL Capital Markets’ Dave Andrews, Pete Pittroff, Michael Scarnato, Michael Lewis and Jack Barnes led negotiations on behalf of the sellers. The post 814K-SF Spartanburg Industrial Park Trades for $99.5M appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Invesco Real Estate bought Crossroads Logistics Park, Spartanburg SC for $99.5M; 814K SF, 100% occupied.
Five-year average remaining lease term; located near I-85 corridor connecting Charlotte and Atlanta.
Asset built by Brennan Investment Group (construction started March 2022); 70-acre campus on logistics corridor.
stories.summary: Invesco Real Estate acquired Crossroads Logistics Park, an 814,000-square-foot industrial campus in Spartanburg, South Carolina, for $99.5 million from Brennan Investment Group and Grandview Partners. The property is fully occupied with an average remaining lease term exceeding five years and comprises two 168,480-SF facilities and a 477,360-SF warehouse spanning 70 acres near I-85, a critical link in the Charlotte-Atlanta logistics corridor.
stories.impact: Not directly relevant to multifamily development. The transaction underscores strong logistics asset performance and capital demand in the Carolinas corridor, but does not inform multifamily-specific demand, supply, capital, or cost dynamics.

stories.title: Savills Expands Manhattan Presence with New Lease at 560 Lexington
stories.excerpt: Global real estate advisory firm Savills has signed a lease with Rudin at 560 Lexington Avenue, a 22-story office tower in the Plaza District. In a five-year agreement, Savills will occupy 20,481 square feet across 560 Lexington’s entire third floor. Savills is expanding its New York City footprint with a new office located blocks from its U.S. headquarters at 399 Park Ave. With this lease, Rudin has completed more than 110,000 square feet of deals at 560 Lexington in 2026. “We’re thrilled to welcome Savills, a global leader in real estate, to 560 Lexington,” said Kevin Daly, VP of office leasing at Rudin. “All the recent activity reaffirms Rudin’s ability to attract new tenants and cultivate long-term relationships – a testament to the building’s prime Plaza District location, dedicated ownership and exceptional level of amenities and service.” Savills represented itself in the transaction. Rudin was represented in-house by Daly and Craig Panzirer, SVP, head of office leasing, along with a CBRE team of Brett Shannon, Peter Turchin, Eric Deutsch, Lauren Levy and Jacob Rosenthal. The post Savills Expands Manhattan Presence with New Lease at 560 Lexington appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Savills leased 20,481 SF (entire third floor) at 560 Lexington, Manhattan for five-year term.
Rudin has completed 110K+ SF of leases at 560 Lexington in 2026; Plaza District location.
Office tower leasing activity reflects Plaza District tenant demand; no impact on residential market.
stories.summary: Global real estate advisory firm Savills signed a five-year lease for 20,481 square feet (entire third floor) at Rudin's 560 Lexington Avenue, a 22-story office tower in Manhattan's Plaza District. With this lease, Rudin has completed more than 110,000 square feet of deals at the building in 2026. Savills is expanding its New York City footprint with this location, which sits blocks from its U.S. headquarters.
stories.impact: Not directly relevant to multifamily development. Office leasing velocity in Manhattan Plaza District signals corporate tenant confidence and capital allocation to office, but does not affect multifamily demand, supply, capital availability, or rents in NYC or other major metros.

stories.title: MOB Investors Favor Income as Capital Markets Regain Momentum
stories.excerpt: The medical office building sector entered 2026 with growing momentum, supported by improving capital markets, greater lender appetite and resilient fundamentals. Cushman & Wakefield’s MOB Capital Markets Mid-Year 2026 Update found that increasing capital flows into healthcare real estate, demographic tailwinds and consistent long-term performance drove investor demand during the first half of the year, setting the stage for continued activity through the remainder of 2026. Investment Accelerates MOB investment volume reached $6.7 billion in the first half of 2026, a 21% increase from a year earlier. Despite a 15% decline in transaction count, the average deal size rose to $20 million, underscoring “continued investor preference for larger, institutional-quality opportunities,” Cushman & Wakefield said. Cap-rate compression also pointed to firmer asset pricing and increased competition. Investors remain attracted to MOB because of steady rent growth, tight supply and high occupancy. Rents increased 2% year over year, although inflation is beginning to outpace rent growth, Cushman & Wakefield said. Debt Market Dynamics Capital availability for MOB investments also improved, with loan origination volume increasing 88% year over year amid stronger investment demand and transaction activity. Banks remain the dominant source of MOB debt, accounting for nearly three-quarters of loan originations over the past five years. Fixed debt costs remained 80 basis points below their 2023 peak, while lenders have shown greater willingness to accept fixed-rate risk and higher loan-to-value ratios. The sector also remains attractive to lenders because of its resilient fundamentals, consistent income returns and positive cash flow. Income returns have remained above 5.5% for seven consecutive quarters, while appreciation returns have turned positive, according to Cushman & Wakefield. bullets: MOB investment volume reached $6.7B in 1H 2026, up 21% year-over-year; average deal size rose to $20M.
Cap-rate compression and tight supply; rents grew 2% YoY but inflation outpacing growth.
Loan origination volume for MOB increased 88% YoY; institutional-quality, larger deals favored by investors.
stories.summary: The medical office building (MOB) sector posted $6.7 billion in investment volume in the first half of 2026, a 21% increase year-over-year, despite a 15% decline in transaction count. Average deal size rose to $20 million, reflecting investor preference for larger, institutional-quality opportunities. Cap-rate compression and tight supply drive investment, though 2% year-over-year rent growth is being outpaced by inflation. Loan origination volume increased 88% year-over-year.
stories.impact: Not directly relevant to multifamily development. MOB capital inflows and improved lending appetite reflect broader healthcare real estate strength, but do not materially affect multifamily capital flows, construction costs, or demand unless significant capital re-allocates from multifamily to MOB in specific metros (no evidence here).

stories.title: Stratford Partners JV Buys San Diego-Area Apartments for $34M
stories.excerpt: A joint venture between Stratford Partners and LLJ has acquired a 189-unit apartment complex in northern San Diego County. The joint venture put down $33.6 million for Pacifica Palms Apartments at 1861 East Washington Avenue in Escondido, according to Institutional Property Advisors (IPA), a division of Marcus & Millichap. The deal works out to about $178,000 per unit. An entity named Pacifica Palms LLC, run by David J. Snodgrass and Barbara Snodgrass, sold the property, records with PropertyShark show. The gated Pacifica Palms includes 20 buildings across 8 acres on East Washington Avenue, about 2.5 miles from Downtown Escondido. The development was completed more than 60 years ago. IPA’s Chris Zorbas and Alexander Garcia Jr. represented the seller and procured the buyer. Zorbas described the property as a rare chance to acquire a large value-add multifamily asset in a supply-constrained submarket. “The Escondido submarket has seen limited availability of multifamily assets of this size,” Zorbas said in a statement. Garcia pointed to the widening cost gap between renting and owning, as Escondido home prices have increased 19 percent since 2021, according to IPA. “The disparity between monthly living expenses for renting versus owning should sustain low vacancy and place upward pressure on Escondido’s rental prices for the foreseeable future,” Garcia said. San Diego’s multifamily market remains tight, with vacancy at 4.2 percent earlier this year, and average effective rents of $2,832 per month, according to Marcus & Millichap’s most recent multifamily report. Deal flow also improved by 25 percent during the 12 months ending in March. Escondido is among the tighter, more affordable submarkets, where limited vacancy is expected to persist. Gregory Cornfield can be reached at gcornfield@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Stratford Partners-LLJ JV acquired 189-unit Pacifica Palms Apartments, Escondido for $33.6M ($178K/unit).
Property is 60+ years old, gated complex on 8 acres; supply-constrained Escondido submarket.
Broker emphasized value-add opportunity and limited multifamily availability in northern San Diego County.
stories.summary: A joint venture between Stratford Partners and LLJ acquired Pacifica Palms Apartments, a 189-unit complex in Escondido (northern San Diego County), for $33.6 million, or approximately $178,000 per unit. The gated property, built over 60 years ago, comprises 20 buildings across 8 acres on East Washington Avenue. The transaction was positioned as a value-add opportunity in a supply-constrained submarket with limited multifamily asset availability.
stories.impact: Escondido submarket tightness and investor appetite for 189-unit value-add assets signal strong demand for older, repositionable multifamily stock in supply-constrained San Diego County submarkets. The $178K/unit price and positioning as rare supply-constrained opportunity underscore robust conditions for repositioning and organic rent growth—encouraging ground-up or stabilized acquisitions in San Diego metro.

stories.title: Walmart Inks Deal at New Miami-Dade Warehouse
stories.excerpt: Walmart has signed an industrial lease in Miami-Dade County, likely spanning more than 130,000 square feet. The retail giant inked a deal at Seagis Property Group’s newly completed warehouse at 10900 Northwest 138th Street in Medley, facing West Okeechobee Road near the Florida Turnpike, property records show. The 16-year lease includes three five-year extensions. Public documents suggest the tenant will occupy the entire 130,150-square-foot property, which rises 40 feet tall and includes two drive-in doors and 46 dock-high doors. A spokesperson for Walmart declined to comment. A representative for the landlord did not respond to requests for comment. Seagis Property Group completed the warehouse this year after buying the 13.2-acre site for $17.5 million in 2022. In another recent South Florida deal, Bentonville, Ark.-based Walmart bought a 24-acre parcel in Palm Beach County for $11.7 million in August to build a superstore. Walmart also renewed its 83,342-square-foot industrial lease at 1981 North Powerline Road in Pompano Beach late last year, according to a market report from Cushman & Wakefield. Julia Echikson can be reached at jechikson@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Walmart signed 16-year lease (plus three 5-year extensions) for 130K+ SF warehouse in Medley, Miami-Dade.
Seagis Property Group developed property completed in 2026; site acquired for $17.5M in 2022.
Location on West Okeechobee Road near Florida Turnpike; part of Walmart's broader South Florida logistics expansion.
stories.summary: Walmart signed a 16-year lease with three five-year extension options for a 130,150-square-foot warehouse at Seagis Property Group's newly completed facility at 10900 Northwest 138th Street in Medley, Miami-Dade County. The property features 40-foot height, 46 dock-high doors, and two drive-in doors. Seagis acquired the 13.2-acre site in 2022 for $17.5 million and completed development in 2026.
stories.impact: Not directly relevant to multifamily development, but Walmart's continued South Florida logistics expansion (warehouse lease + 24-acre Palm Beach County acquisition) signals strong regional logistics demand and capital deployment. This may compete with multifamily land acquisition in Miami-Dade and Palm Beach submarkets and reinforce industrial-to-multifamily land zoning/entitlement challenges.

stories.title: Global Wellness Network Havas Health Expands to 254K SF at 200 Madison Avenue
stories.excerpt: Havas Health, a global health and wellness communications network, is expanding its Midtown headquarters, Commercial Observer has learned. Havas, which creates advertising, public relations and marketing campaigns for health care brands, signed a 15-year deal to renew its existing 189,461-square-foot office at George Comfort & Sons’ 200 Madison Avenue and tack on an additional 64,657 square feet, according to the landlord. The deal, which stretches through at least 2041, brings the health company’s total footprint to 254,118 square feet across five floors of the 26-story office building seven blocks south of Grand Central Terminal. Asking rents for available office space in the building — which George Comfort owns alongside Loeb Partners Realty and Jamestown — average $70 to $75 per square foot, according to ownership. Founded in 1835, Havas is one of the world’s largest global communications groups and has been a tenant at 200 Madison Avenue since the late 1990s. “Havas Health’s growing long-term commitment to 200 Madison Avenue is a testament to the appeal of the hospitality-focused, amenity-rich environment we are cultivating for our tenants,” Peter Duncan, president and CEO of George Comfort, said in a statement. “Havas has been a valued tenant for nearly three decades, and we are proud to support its next chapter of success within the tower.” Duncan and Alexander Bermingham represented ownership in-house in the deal, while Newmark’s David Falk and Jason Greenstein repped the tenant. A spokesperson for Newmark did not immediately respond to a request for comment. George Comfort recently completed a renovation of the office tower’s entrance and lobby, and it is in the midst of building a new indoor-outdoor amenity center on the 10th floor, which will span 11,000 square feet and feature conference rooms, a game area, a lounge and event spaces. The center will also include an outdoor garden, according to the landlord. Other tenants at 200 Madison Avenue i
bullets: Havas Health renewed 189.5K SF and added 64.7K SF at 200 Madison Avenue, Manhattan; 15-year deal through 2041.
Total footprint expands to 254.1K SF across five floors; rents $70–$75/SF at building.
Long-term tenant (since late 1990s) committing to Midtown office; reflects healthcare-marketing sector demand.
stories.summary: Havas Health, a global health and wellness communications network, signed a 15-year lease renewal and expansion at George Comfort & Sons' 200 Madison Avenue in Midtown Manhattan. The deal renews Havas's existing 189,461-square-foot footprint and adds 64,657 square feet, bringing the tenant's total to 254,118 square feet across five floors through 2041. Asking rents at the building average $70 to $75 per square foot.
stories.impact: Not directly relevant to multifamily development. Office tenant retention and expansion in Midtown Manhattan signal corporate capital commitment to NYC office, but does not materially affect multifamily capital flows, supply, or rents unless large-scale office-to-residential conversions accelerate (not evident here).

stories.title: T30 Capital Sells East Williamsburg Loft Building at 59 Bogart Street for $30M
stories.excerpt: Local real estate investor Jo-Ann Obergfell is buying a 51-unit multifamily property in East Williamsburg, Brooklyn. The low-profile Obergfell, using the LLC 59 Bogart tied to an address in Brooklyn, acquired 59 Bogart Street from T30 Capital for $30 million, according to property records and seller broker CBRE. Originally an industrial property, the three-story building was converted to residential lofts in 2005. “We experienced tremendous demand for this asset as capital continues to seek value-add properties in active investment markets,” CBRE’s Robert Shapiro, who negotiated the deal alongside Ian Brooks, said in a statement. “The property attracted significant investor interest due to its transit-oriented location, recent residential conversion and proximity to major planned development projects.” Obergfell, who has served as president of Ellio’s Pizza and G.A. Productions, could not be reached for comment. She signed the deed filing as the authorized signatory of 59 Bogart LLC. Jeremy Salzberg, co-founder and managing partner of T30 Capital, signed on behalf of the firm, listing the headquarters of the firm as the mailing address for the shell corporation 59 Bogart Owner, as well as signing for two other organizations listed as under the seller. T30 Capital is linked to affiliate Sugar Hill Capital Partners, which serves as its property-owning predecessor entity and bought 59 Bogart Street — also known as 315 Seigel Street — for $39.5 million in 2016. All new business, investments and operations are conducted directly through T30 Capital. The property situated above the L train’s Morgan Avenue station offers one- to three-bedroom units, along with a lounge, a gym, a bike room and communal outdoor spaces for residents, according to CBRE. Mark Hallum can be reached at mhallum@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Jo-Ann Obergfell (via 59 Bogart LLC) acquired 51-unit multifamily loft building, East Williamsburg for $30M.
Property converted from industrial to residential in 2005; transit-oriented, near planned development projects.
T30 Capital seller; CBRE noted strong demand for value-add assets in active investment markets.
stories.summary: Local real estate investor Jo-Ann Obergfell acquired 59 Bogart Street, a 51-unit multifamily loft building in East Williamsburg, Brooklyn, from T30 Capital for $30 million. Originally industrial, the three-story building was converted to residential lofts in 2005. CBRE brokers noted significant investor demand driven by the property's transit-oriented location, recent residential conversion, and proximity to major planned development projects.
stories.impact: Strong investor appetite for 51-unit value-add residential assets in East Williamsburg signals tight Williamsburg-Greenpoint supply and robust rent-growth fundamentals. Proximity to planned development projects (likely includes rezoning/new housing) reinforces near-term scarcity premium and entry opportunity window—encouraging ground-up or stabilized multifamily acquisitions in Brooklyn submarkets before supply pipeline densifies.
